editorial.headline: Private Language Education: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers private language courses and related test-preparation and translator training, open at every business scale with full foreign ownership nationally.
editorial.body:
Private language education is a course-based activity designed to build language skills and expertise, delivered by private providers. Its practical field is broad: Arabic, Dutch, Indonesian, English, Italian, Javanese, Japanese, German, Korean, Mandarin, French, Russian, Sakura, Spanish and other languages all sit within the stated scope. It also includes courses for TOEFL, TOEIC and IELTS, alongside translator courses. This is therefore an educational activity focused on language capability and assessment or translation-oriented training, rather than a general description of schooling.

The activity is open to micro, small, medium and large enterprises. That matters because the record does not reserve private language-course provision to one narrow commercial scale: the same activity can be registered across the full stated range, from Mikro through Besar. For a founder, the defining question is whether the business genuinely delivers the course-based language education described here—whether through a named language, proficiency-test preparation, or translator training.

Nationally, the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership at the national level for this activity. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national position is unusually direct: the record does not attach a lower foreign-equity ceiling to this activity.

Bali’s picture is also clear, but it should be read on its own terms. The provincial moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA registration across the island on a permanent basis. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium because, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Bali’s status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: the activity is not screened out under the moratorium, while its large-scale risk position remains central to that conclusion. For a foreign-owned private language-education business, Bali is not a false promise or a blanket prohibition in this record; it is an available route outside the moratorium’s blocked risk bands.
